patients.summary: Graduate student with genetically confirmed Marfan syndrome and bilateral ectopia lentis who joins in 2022 on metoprolol and aspirin. A 2024 echo finds a 4.2 cm aortic root and severe aortic regurgitation managed medically; a 2025 right lens subluxation and a February 2026 type A dissection repaired with a valve-sparing root and hemiarch replacement follow.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
25 y/o man here to establish. Started a master's in library sciences this fall, lives in an apartment near downtown.

Hx: Marfan syndrome. Dad was diagnosed in his late 30s and had his aortic root replaced prophylactically at 38 (composite valve-graft); the family was tested after that and Silas carries the same FBN1 variant. Younger sister also positive, followed by her own cardiologist. Paternal uncle died suddenly at 31 -- family has always assumed a dissection. Mom healthy, tested negative.
Both lenses have been partly dislocated since he was a kid; wears glasses, eye exams were through a pediatric ophthalmologist and lapsed after high school.
Saw a pediatric cardiologist through his teens who put him on metoprolol succinate 50 and a baby aspirin. Thinks his last echo was freshman year of college. No echo or CT since. Feels fine. No chest pain, no dyspnea, no palpitations, no syncope. Plays pickup ultimate occasionally.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: none to medications.
Surg: none.
Social: never smoker, a drink or two a month, no drugs. Single.

Exam: very tall, slender. Long fingers, arm span looks longer than height. Chest wall normal on inspection.Heart RRR, no murmur appreciated today. Lungs clear. Pupils round, glasses on. No edema.

A/P
1. Marfan syndrome with FBN1 variant -- he is overdue for aortic imaging by a few years. Referral to adult cardiology for echo and ongoing surveillance. Continue metoprolol. Talked about avoiding heavy lifting/straining and competitive contact sports until cardiology weighs in.
2. Ectopia lentis -- suggested he get back in with an eye doctor; he'll look for one his insurance covers.
3. Aspirin -- continue for now, will let cardiology decide whether it's needed.
Records release signed for the pediatric cardiology and genetics offices.
Physical in about a year.

documents.title: Prior pediatric cardiology and genetics records
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Received 14 pages from the patient's former pediatric cardiology practice, including a clinical genetics letter. Summary for the chart: genetic testing in adolescence found a pathogenic FBN1 variant (same variant as father); clinical diagnosis of Marfan syndrome with bilateral ectopia lentis. Started on metoprolol succinate and low-dose aspirin by the pediatric cardiologist. Immunizations through childhood complete per their records. Last clinic note is from the patient's first year of college; no measurements abstracted. Scanned under Media. Routed to PCP.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Physical. Second year of the program, working at the campus archives part time. No complaints. Walks everywhere, no exercise limitation. Denies chest discomfort, shortness of breath, fainting, palpitations. Vision stable with his glasses; hasn't found an eye doctor yet.

Never got to cardiology -- the referral timed out in the spring. We talked again about why it matters given his dad's and uncle's history. He says he'll call himself once his assistantship schedule settles; I gave him the number again rather than re-placing it today.

Meds metoprolol succinate 50, aspirin 81, taking both. NKDA.
PHQ-2 0.

Exam: tall thin young man in no distress. HEENT normal, glasses. Neck supple. Heart regular, I don't hear a murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abd soft. Long fingers and limbs. Skin no rashes. Neuro grossly normal.

Plan
- CMP, CBC, lipids; one-time HIV and hep C screens -- he agreed.
- Tdap today (unsure when last), flu, updated covid.
- Cardiology: patient to self-schedule, gave number.
- Eye care: list of in-network ophthalmologists in AVS.
- See back in a year.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Came in because he's been running out of gas. Over the last few months more tired than usual and gets winded climbing to the 4th floor stacks, which never used to bother him. Every so often feels his heart racing, and at night lying down he can feel it pounding in his chest. No chest pain, no fainting, no leg swelling, no fevers. Sleeping ok.
Unrelated: had a molar pulled earlier this month; the dentist had him take an antibiotic beforehand because of the Marfan.
Still hasn't seen cardiology.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 daily, ASA 81. NKDA.

O: BP and HR as charted -- note diastolic is low, pulse pressure wide. Pulses bounding at the wrists. Heart: there's a murmur today along the left sternal border that I did not hear on prior exams. Lungs clear, no crackles. No JVD. No peripheral edema. Thin, long limbs.

A/P: Exertional fatigue/dyspnea with palpitations, new murmur and wide pulse pressure in a 26 yo with Marfan -- worried about the aortic root and aortic valve. Urgent cardiology referral placed today, and I called their office myself to get him in within 2 weeks. CBC, BMP, TSH to look for anything else contributing. Told him no heavy lifting, and to go straight to the ED for chest, back or abdominal pain, fainting, or sudden shortness of breath. He understood and seemed more motivated this time.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Blood count, kidney function, electrolytes and thyroid all came back normal, so no anemia or thyroid problem behind the fatigue. Cardiology has you on 2/6 -- please keep that one.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CARDIOLOGY GROUP -- CONSULTATION
Date of service: 02/06/2024
Referring: primary care physician

Reason for consultation: fatigue and exertional dyspnea, Marfan syndrome.

History: 26-year-old graduate student with FBN1-positive Marfan syndrome and bilateral lens subluxation, without cardiology follow-up since early college. Over several months he has noticed progressive tiredness and breathlessness with exertion. He describes intermittent palpitations and an uncomfortable awareness of a forceful heartbeat when he lies flat. No exertional chest pain or syncope.

Medications: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily; aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Surgical history: dental extraction January 2024 with antibiotic prophylaxis from his dentist.
Family history: father with Marfan syndrome who underwent prophylactic aortic root replacement at 38; paternal uncle died suddenly at 31, presumed dissection; mother well; younger sister with Marfan syndrome, under surveillance.
Social: never smoker; alcohol 1-2 drinks per month; graduate student in library sciences.

Examination: BP 140/45 mmHg. Pulse 90, bounding character. Height 193 cm. Arachnodactyly; arm span greater than height. A murmur is present on auscultation. Fundi normal on fundoscopy. Lungs clear. No edema.

Impression: Marfan syndrome with symptoms and a hyperdynamic circulation that raise concern for aortic root enlargement with aortic valve incompetence.

Plan: transthoracic echocardiogram, scheduled 2/21. Continue current medications. Follow-up after the study.

Thank you for this referral.
Cardiology

reports.text:
Indication: Marfan syndrome, murmur, wide pulse pressure.
Technically adequate study.
Left ventricle: normal size and wall thickness. Normal systolic function, LVEF 60% by biplane method. No regional wall motion abnormality.
Right ventricle: normal size and function.
Atria: normal size.
Aortic valve: trileaflet. Chronic severe aortic regurgitation, central jet.
Aortic root: dilated, 4.2 cm at the sinuses, measured leading edge to leading edge in end-diastole. Ascending aorta normal caliber.
Mitral valve: prolapse of the mitral leaflets with mild mitral regurgitation.
Tricuspid and pulmonic valves: normal.
Pericardium: no effusion.
IVC normal size with normal respiratory variation.
reports.conclusion: Dilated aortic root 4.2 cm. Chronic severe aortic regurgitation. Mitral valve prolapse with mild mitral regurgitation. Normal LV size and function, LVEF 60%.

documents.author: cardiology

OUTSIDE CARDIOLOGY GROUP -- FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 02/29/2024

Silas returns to review his echocardiogram of 2/21.

Findings reviewed with him: aortic root measures 4.2 cm at the sinuses; chronic severe aortic regurgitation; mitral valve prolapse with mild mitral regurgitation; left ventricle normal in size with LVEF 60%.

Assessment:
1. Marfan syndrome (FBN1) with aortic root aneurysm, 4.2 cm.
2. Chronic severe aortic regurgitation.
3. Mitral valve prolapse, mild MR.

Plan:
- Start lisinopril 10 mg daily for afterload reduction; continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and aspirin 81 mg daily.
- Avoid heavy lifting, straining and competitive or contact sports.
- BMP with his primary care physician in 3-4 weeks after starting lisinopril.
- Repeat echocardiogram in 6 months.
- Go to an emergency department for sudden chest, back or abdominal pain, or fainting.

Medications at end of visit: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Cardiology

documents.title: RE: Echo results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good questions. I got their letter. The root is enlarged and the valve leak is significant, which is why they added lisinopril alongside your metoprolol and want a repeat echo in 6 months -- that's how they'll watch it. Let's go over it in person when you come in for the blood test in a few weeks; I put you down for 3/26. Same warning signs as before: sudden chest or back pain or fainting means the ER, not a message.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up after his cardiology workup. Echo 2/21: aortic root 4.2 cm, chronic severe AR, MVP with mild MR, EF 60%. Lisinopril 10 added 2/29.

Taking all three meds. No cough, no lightheadedness on standing. Energy about the same, still some breathlessness on stairs. No chest or back pain.

BP better than January though diastolic still low, as expected with the leak. Diastolic murmur LSB. Lungs clear. No edema.

We spent most of the visit on what this means -- the root and valve will be followed with echoes, and I explained the reasons for no heavy lifting. He asked about his sister; told him her cardiologist is the right person for her screening. BMP today for K and creatinine on the ACE inhibitor.

Problem list updated with cardiology's diagnoses. Continue metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 10, aspirin 81. Physical in the fall.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record

documents.body:
EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN DOCUMENTATION -- outside hospital
Arrival 02/12/2025 07:05

CC: R eye vision changed this AM

HPI: 27M with Marfan syndrome and known bilateral lens subluxation, evaluated by cardiology about a year ago for aortic regurgitation. Woke up, rubbed his right eye lightly, and his vision in that eye abruptly shifted -- blurry and "off." No injury beyond the rub. No eye pain. No headache.

PMH: Marfan syndrome (FBN1); aortic root aneurysm 4.2 cm; chronic severe AR; MVP with mild MR, diagnosed last year; bilateral ectopia lentis. Tall with long extremities.
PSH: dental extraction 2024 (antibiotic prophylaxis).
Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: father Marfan, prophylactic root replacement at 38; paternal uncle sudden death at 31, presumed dissection; mother healthy; younger sister with Marfan.
SHx: never smoker; EtOH 1-2/month; graduate student, library sciences.

Exam:
VS: BP 130/70, HR 78, afebrile.
General: 6'4", arm span exceeds height, comfortable.
Eyes: right lens displaced up and toward the nose. Conjunctiva white, no injection. Fluorescein: no corneal abrasion. No redness.
CV: midsystolic click, then a late systolic murmur at the apex.
Remainder of exam unremarkable.

MDM: painless acute visual change from progression of known right lens subluxation after minor rubbing. No signs of trauma, globe injury or angle closure. Habitus marfanoid, consistent with his known diagnosis.

Impression: right ectopia lentis, acute progression of subluxation.
Disposition: home. Eye shield not required. Ophthalmology referral for urgent visit, appointment arranged for 2/14. Return for eye pain, red eye, worsening vision, flashes, floaters or a curtain over vision.

Emergency medicine attending

documents.title: Ophthalmology Consultation
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Ophthalmology consultation, 02/14/2025. Seen at the request of the emergency department; copy to primary care.

Thank you for sending Mr. Morrow, a 27-year-old with Marfan syndrome and bilateral ectopia lentis since childhood, seen two days ago in the ED after his right vision shifted on rubbing the eye. No pain.

Examination: right lens subluxated superonasally, more than the left. The left lens subluxation appears stable from his description of childhood findings. Both lenses remain behind the iris; no lens in the anterior chamber or vitreous. Intraocular pressure normal in both eyes. Anterior chambers quiet. Dilated fundus exam: retina attached in both eyes, no tears or holes, optic nerves healthy.

Assessment: bilateral ectopia lentis, recent progression on the right.

Plan: refraction updated and new spectacle prescription provided. Observation. He should avoid rubbing his eyes. Lens surgery would be considered only if his vision cannot be adequately corrected with glasses. Return immediately for flashes, new floaters or a curtain in his vision. Recheck in 6 months.

Meds reviewed: metoprolol succinate, lisinopril, aspirin. Allergies: NKDA.

Ophthalmology

conditions.label: Dissection of ascending aorta
conditions.note: acute type A, root through ascending aorta into proximal arch

reports.text: Portable AP chest. The mediastinum is widened. Lungs are clear. No pneumothorax. No pleural effusion. Bony thorax intact.

CT angiography of the chest with IV contrast, dissection protocol.
An intimal flap begins at the aortic root and extends through the ascending aorta into the proximal aortic arch. Aortic root measures 4.2 cm. The descending thoracic aorta is normal in caliber without a flap. No pericardial effusion. No mediastinal hematoma beyond the aortic wall. Lungs clear; no pleural effusion.
reports.conclusion: Acute type A aortic dissection from the aortic root into the proximal arch.

OUTSIDE HOSPITAL ED -- PHYSICIAN NOTE
Arrived by ambulance 02/13/2026 09:31

Chief complaint: acute upper back pain.

HPI: 28-year-old man with Marfan syndrome and a known thoracic aortic root aneurysm, followed for aortic regurgitation since 2024 and seen here in 2025 for a lens problem in his right eye. Brought in after abrupt, severe pain between the shoulder blades that started while he was sitting at his desk. He calls it sharp and ripping.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 10 mg, aspirin 81 mg daily. NKDA.
PSH: dental extraction 2024.
FHx: father with Marfan, aortic root replaced at 38; paternal uncle died suddenly at 31, thought to be dissection; sister with Marfan.
Social: never smoker; rare alcohol; graduate student.

Exam: Temp 36.7 C. BP 88/40 right arm, 112/44 left arm. HR 112. Tall, thin, limbs and fingers disproportionately long. Heart: high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur, loudest at the left sternal border. Lungs clear.

Course: two large-bore IVs. Portable chest film with a wide mediastinum. Cardiothoracic surgery at the tertiary center called before CT. CT angiogram: acute type A dissection from the root into the proximal arch. CBC, BMP and high-sensitivity troponin within normal limits. Aspirin held. Accepted in transfer by cardiac surgery; left by critical care transport at 13:55.

Diagnosis: acute type A aortic dissection.
Allergies: NKDA.

Emergency medicine attending

documents.title: Discharge Summary -- Cardiac Surgery
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
TERTIARY CARE CENTER -- CARDIAC SURGERY DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 02/13/2026 (transfer from outside ED). Discharged 02/20/2026.

Principal diagnosis: acute type A aortic dissection.
Background: Marfan syndrome (FBN1); aortic root aneurysm 4.2 cm; chronic severe aortic regurgitation; mitral valve prolapse with mild MR; bilateral ectopia lentis.

Operation 02/13/2026: emergency valve-sparing aortic root replacement (reimplantation) with hemiarch replacement, via median sternotomy, under cardiopulmonary bypass with circulatory arrest for the hemiarch. Native aortic valve preserved. Intraoperative TEE after repair: trace aortic regurgitation, LVEF 55%.

Hospital course: extubated postoperative day 1. ICU through day 2, then step-down. Chest tubes out day 3. Pain controlled with oral acetaminophen. Ambulating independently by day 4. Uneventful recovery.

Discharge medications:
- metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily
- lisinopril 10 mg daily
- aspirin 81 mg daily (resumed)
- acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed for pain

Allergies: NKDA.

Instructions: sternal precautions -- no lifting over 10 lb, no pushing or pulling, no driving for 6 weeks. Keep the incision clean and dry. Referral placed to outpatient cardiac rehabilitation. Cardiac surgery clinic in about 5 weeks. Primary care within 2 weeks. Call or return for fever, wound drainage, chest or back pain, or shortness of breath.

Cardiac surgery

Pain 3/10, using acetaminophen once or twice a day. Incision dry, no redness or drainage. No fever. Walking around the house several times a day. Has all 3 heart meds plus Tylenol, reviewed against discharge list -- matches. Knows sternal precautions. Parents driving him. Booked with PCP 3/3, surgery clinic letter says late March. Reviewed when to call 911.

events.reason: Hospital follow-up after aortic dissection repair

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospital follow-up. Discharge summary and outside ED record reviewed.
2/13 sudden ripping interscapular pain at his desk; outside ED: BP 88/40 R, 112/44 L, HR 112, new early diastolic murmur, wide mediastinum on CXR; CTA type A dissection root to proximal arch. Transferred, emergency valve-sparing root reimplantation + hemiarch the same evening. TEE afterward trace AR, EF 55%. Home 2/20.

Now: dad drove him in. Sore at the sternum, acetaminophen a couple times a day. Walking 15-20 min twice daily. First cardiac rehab session was yesterday. No fever, no wound drainage, no new back or chest pain, no shortness of breath.
Meds: metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 10, aspirin 81, acetaminophen PRN. Matches the discharge list.

Exam: looks tired but well. BP and HR as charted -- pulse pressure normal now. Sternotomy incision intact, edges together, no erythema or drainage; sternum stable. Heart regular, I don't hear the old diastolic murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. Weight down a few pounds from the hospital stay.

A/P
1. Type A aortic dissection s/p valve-sparing root + hemiarch replacement -- recovering on schedule. Updated the problem list: root aneurysm and AR marked resolved with the repair; dissection kept. Continue meds. Sternal precautions until 6 weeks. Surgery clinic 3/25.
2. Marfan syndrome / MVP / ectopia lentis -- unchanged.
3. Spent time on how he's coping -- shaken, but has family around; he knows to reach out.
See me again in about 5-6 weeks.

Plan: may advance activity per cardiac rehab and resume driving. Lifelong avoidance of heavy lifting and straining (isometric exertion). Continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 10 mg, aspirin 81 mg. Surveillance CT angiogram of the chest at about 6 months after surgery; ongoing care with his cardiologist.

8 wk out from the type A repair. Surgery clinic 3/25: healed, cleared to drive and progress through rehab, CTA around August.

Drove himself today. Back in his own apartment. Rehab 3x/week, says he feels better than he did before the surgery -- more energy on the stairs. Not taking acetaminophen anymore. No chest or back pain, no palpitations, no swelling. Thesis defense pushed to summer, his advisor has been flexible.
Meds: metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 10, aspirin 81. NKDA.

Exam: well. Sternotomy well healed. RRR, soft systolic click at the apex, no diastolic murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P: s/p aortic dissection repair, doing well. BMP and CBC today. Keep cardiology and CTA in summer. Annual physical in the fall.

OUTSIDE CARDIOLOGY GROUP -- FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 07/16/2026

Five months after emergency valve-sparing root and hemiarch replacement for type A dissection. Finished cardiac rehab. Feels well, no chest or back pain.

CTA 7/8: repair intact, no residual dissection, distal aorta normal caliber.
Echo today: trace AR, LVEF 55%, MVP with mild MR.

Plan: continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 10 mg and aspirin 81 mg daily. Lifelong activity restrictions as discussed. Yearly imaging of the aorta, alternating echo and CTA. Return in 12 months.
Allergies: NKDA.
